extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, librarians, and researchers in media studies and media economics
extracted.subtask_description: Metadata and descriptive summary page for a scholarly book (James T. Hamilton, All the News That's Fit to Sell) that develops an economic theory of news and surveys evidence across media markets. The page provides a summary, table of contents, bibliographic metadata, and the book's main conclusions and policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of story selection (newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story appears in print, on television, or on the Internet depends on who is interested, its value to advertisers, the costs of assembling the details, and competitors' products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit factors cited: audience interest, advertiser value, cost of gathering details, and competitor offerings. The summary uses this as the central model for explaining why some topics become news and others do not. Examples given: shifts in network evening news story selection to attract specific demographic groups (e.g., young female viewers), and the general shift from 'hard' political news toward 'soft' entertainment-oriented stories under competitive pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use economic incentives to evaluate news content
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze news content and journalistic behavior through an economic theory: assess how incentives (market competition, deregulation, ownership changes) affect reporting decisions and content mix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book is described as the first to develop such a theory and to analyze evidence across a range of media markets. Empirical illustrations referenced include: evolution of nonpartisan newspapers (1870–1900), story selection on network evening news programs (1969–1998), local television and local newspapers, and news on the Internet. The page implies evaluation should consider historical and cross-media evidence about how incentives reshape journalistic norms and outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and institutional levers to improve news serving the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended interventions to counteract market-driven degradation of news and to better ensure news serves the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommendations listed: lower costs of access to government information; increase the role of nonprofits in funding journalism; develop norms that stress hard news reporting; and define digital and Internet property rights to encourage the flow of news. These are presented as evaluative standards or remedies for assessing how to improve news ecosystems in light of the book's economic findings.
